newsitem.title: INDIA: India call money ends easier on improved liquidity.
newsitem.headline: India call money ends easier on improved liquidity.

text.p: Indian call money ended Friday easier on improved liquidity with dealers reporting rates of one percent at close of trade. Earlier, call money was quoted in the 2.0-3.0 percent range in opening trade.
Dealers said liquidity with the banking system had improved in the last few days, leading to call money rates coming down from around seven percent in opening trade on Tuesday to the current levels.

Some dealers said the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) dollar purchases had injected rupees into the banking system. The RBI has been buying dollars in recent times in the forex market to prevent the Indian rupee from appreciating.
Call money rates were expected to harden slightly as banks began to divert funds to more profitable investments such as treasury bills.
"There is no reason for surplus funds to float around in the call money market at one to two percent," a dealer said.

"Treasury bills available on tap with the RBI offer 4.6 percent. Some money is likely to go there and we should see call rates move up to around five percent." Dealers said security prices were steady in moderate trade.
"At the moment, everyone seems to be overbought in short-dated securities," said a dealer. "Volumes are not very high...market players are still waiting to see if the current easy liquidity lasts."
The 13.50 percent 1997 government of India stock traded on Friday at 102.70 rupees against its last traded price of 102.62, dealers said.
In longer-dated securities, the 12.50 percent 2004 stock was traded at 94.64 rupees against 94.55.
Dealers said three-month commercial paper by top-rated companies was quoted between 12 percent and 13 percent in the primary market.
